result:
There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes when someone tells you to write freely about whatever you want.

Most writing has a fence around it. Write an essay about the Civil War. Write a product description for a toaster. Write an apology to your landlord. The fence is confining, but it's also comforting. You know where the edges are. You know what would count as failing.

When the fence is removed, the field becomes infinite, and the infinite is paralyzing. Whatever I want? I could write about anything. I could write about the migratory patterns of Arctic terns. I could write about why I still remember the phone number of my childhood house. I could write about toast. And because I could write about anything, I have to confront the question of what I actually *want* to write about, which is a much more personal and revealing question than it first appears.

So let's start there. With the blank page.

A blank page is not empty. That's the first illusion. We think of it as nothing, as a void waiting to be filled. But it's crowded. It's crowded with every possible thing you could put there, all existing at once in superposition. Before you write the first word, you could still be Shakespeare. You could still be brilliant, funny, profound. The moment you commit to a first sentence, you collapse all those possibilities into one actual, flawed reality. Writing is an act of loss. You murder a thousand perfect imaginary essays to birth one imperfect real one.

I think that's why we love watching other people create. To see the first brushstroke go down, or the first line of code compile. There's bravery in it.

I used to have a teacher who told us to start by writing the worst possible sentence we could think of. "The moist goat screamed philosophically at the purple taxes." Something deliberately bad, so that the perfectionism loses its grip. Because you cannot be afraid of ruining a page that already has a screaming goat on it. I still use that trick. My worst sentence for today is: "The toaster was very thoughtful about existentialism on Tuesdays." Okay. Now the page is ruined. Now we can begin.

---

Let me tell you about my favorite place that doesn't exist anymore.

When I was nine or ten, there was a library branch three blocks from my house. It was not a beautiful library. It was a 1970s municipal building, low and brown, with carpet that had a faint smell of old crayons and rain. The adult section and children's section were not really separate; they just sort of bled into each other. The librarians knew my name and not in a cute movie way, but in a slightly tired, "you're here again?" way.

There was an aisle in the back, Dewey Decimal 500s, the science books, that no one ever visited. That's where I lived. The books there were old. 1960s books about THE FUTURE, with illustrations of people in silver jumpsuits eating pills for dinner and living in underwater bubble cities by the year 1999. Which, from the vantage point of 2002, was already a shattered promise. I loved those books desperately because they were so confident and so wrong.

One book had a cutaway diagram of a home of the future. Everything was automated. There was a machine that would pick out your clothes for you. There was a machine that would brush your teeth. I remember staring at that and thinking, I don't want a machine to pick out my clothes. But the idea that someone in 1965 thought we would want it felt intimate, like reading someone's diary.

Libraries are time machines in that way. Not because of the knowledge inside the books, but because every old book is a record of what people used to think they didn't know. A 1960s science book doesn't tell you about science; it tells you about 1960s anxiety about science. A cookbook from 1958 tells you about gender. An atlas from 1922 tells you about empire.

That branch closed when I was twelve. They consolidated it with a bigger, newer, brighter library across town. The new library had computers and natural light and a cafe. It was objectively better in every measurable way. I hated it. And I still dream about the old one sometimes. Not about the books, but about the exact quality of the light coming through the high, narrow windows at 4 p.m. in October, making dust motes visible above the pseudoscience shelf. My brain kept a very high-resolution texture file of a place I only went to for two years.

That seems to be something human memory does. It doesn't save the important things. It saves the wallpaper. It saves the sound the door made. It saves the dust.

---

Have you ever really thought about socks?

No, seriously. Socks are an engineering marvel that we have decided is boring. Consider the problem: you need to wrap a three-dimensional, irregularly shaped, sweaty, mobile object — the human foot — in a soft, washable layer that doesn't bunch, doesn't slip, stays warm but not too warm, can survive being dragged around inside a shoe all day, and can be manufactured for twenty cents. And we solved it. With a tube of knitted cotton and some elastic.

And then we invented the dryer, which is a machine whose secret secondary purpose is to test our faith, because it regularly removes one sock from existence and gives nothing in return.

My grandmother had a theory about lost socks. She said every house has a sock dimension, a small wrinkle in space behind the dryer where all the missing socks live and have a better life without us. I like that much better than the entropy explanation. The physicist would tell you socks get lost because disorder increases; there are many more ways for socks to be separated than for them to be together, so statistically, separation is inevitable. The universe tends towards unpaired socks. That's the second law of thermodynamics.

But I prefer the small society of liberated socks behind the wall, finally free of feet.

Entropy is one of those ideas that, once you see it, you can't unsee it. My coffee gets cold. My bedroom gets messy. My body gets older. The effort it takes to keep anything together — a relationship, a houseplant, a sourdough starter — is always slightly more than you expect, because you are swimming upstream against the entire universe's preference for scattering.

And yet, we do it. We make beds. We pair socks. We keep the sourdough alive. That's maybe the most human thing. Knowing the tendency and doing the work anyway.

---

I want to talk about the ocean for a moment, because if I'm allowed to write about whatever I want, I want to write about water.

Most people live their lives on land and think of the ocean as a place you visit. But if you look at a real map of the Earth — not the political map, but the physical one — the planet is ocean with some islands in it. The Pacific alone covers more area than all the land combined. We live on the exception, not the rule.

I went to the Atlantic for the first time when I was seven and I was terrified in a way I didn't have language for. It wasn't that it was big. Big I could understand. It was that it was indifferent. It was there before me and it would be there after, and it did not want anything from me. A mountain wants you to climb it. A forest wants you to get lost in it, or at least it feels like it does. The ocean just is. The waves don't care if you are watching.

Standing at the edge of it, I understood, for the first time, what people mean when they say God is not necessarily kind. They don't mean cruel. They mean vast and operating on a scale where kindness as we understand it doesn't apply. The ocean isn't cruel. It drowns people because water doesn't breathe. That's not cruelty. That's physics.

And still, we love it. We go back to it. We put our children in it. We write songs about it. Maybe because that indifference is restful. For once, nothing loves you or hates you. It just holds you for a second if you know how to float.

I learned to float late. I was fourteen at a local pool, and a lifeguard who was tired of watching me thrash around finally just put his hand under my back and said, "Stop doing so much. The water already knows how to hold you." And it did.

---

There is a list I keep in my head of small human inventions that are perfect.

The paperclip. The zipper. The window screen. The sticky note. The teaspoon.

None of these people got famous in the way we reserve for inventors of cars or phones. But someone had to look at a stack of papers that kept blowing away and think, I could bend a wire in a very particular way. That's genius of a quieter kind.

I think we are entering an age where we are obsessed with big, world-breaking invention. Disruptive technology. Moonshots. Move fast and break things. I am nostalgic for the paperclip inventors. The people who wanted to make one small corner of daily life 2% less annoying and succeeded.

My favorite perfect thing is the library due-date card pocket. You know, before barcodes, when they had a little manila pocket glued inside the front cover and they'd stamp a card. Some anonymous person designed that pocket, determined its exact dimensions, figured out the best glue so it wouldn't yellow the first page. How many billions of little pockets were glued in? How many hands touched them? That person contributed more to human happiness than most CEOs, and we don't know their name.

If I could write about whatever I want, I want to write a thank-you note to all those people.

To the person who invented the little plastic table that goes in the middle of a pizza so the box doesn't touch the cheese. Thank you.

To whoever decided that manhole covers should be round so they can't fall through their own hole. Thank you, you're clever.

To the woman in the 1940s who invented the chocolate chip cookie by accident because she ran out of baker's chocolate. Thank you.

---

Let's talk about the future for a second, because the old science books got it so wrong, and we're getting it wrong right now too.

When I was a kid, the future was going to be flying cars and robot butlers. We are now living in what is, by any 1960s standard, the future, and we have supercomputers in our pockets that can access all of human knowledge and we mostly use them to argue about whether a dress is blue or gold and to watch videos of a dog stealing a sandwich. Which is probably what humans would do in any future.

I think we keep predicting the wrong things because we predict technologies, not feelings. We thought we'd want pill-food because it's efficient. But we didn't factor in that humans love chewing. We love ritual. We love the smell of bread. Efficiency was never the point.

So what will the next fifty years actually feel like? I don't know. I suspect we will still have laundry. I suspect we will still lose socks. I suspect we will have some astonishing new ability — maybe to print organs, maybe to translate dolphin — and we will incorporate it into our lives so quickly that within five years it will feel boring. Humans are incredible at normalization. The miracle becomes the background.

In 1850, if you told someone you could turn on a light in your house at midnight without a candle, they'd call you a wizard. Now if my kitchen light takes half a second longer than usual to turn on, I am annoyed at it. That is both a flaw and a feature.

The part of the future I am most interested in is not what tools we will have, but what we will still choose to do by hand even when we don't have to. We still bake bread even though we can buy it. We still hike even though we have cars. We still write letters by hand sometimes. Those are clues to what is actually essential.

Maybe in fifty years we will have machines that can write any song perfectly, instantly, in any style. And therefore the most valuable song will be the imperfect one your friend recorded in one take in her bedroom, with a dog barking in the background. Because it will prove a human made it.

Handmade things will not be about quality. They will be about proof of effort, proof of life.

---

I realize I've been jumping around. From blank pages to libraries to socks to oceans to paperclips to the future. That is what free writing actually looks like, I think. Not a straight road, but a wandering. Your mind doesn't walk in a straight line unless you force it.

If you sit quietly and just follow the actual associative path of your thoughts for five minutes, you will end up somewhere completely bizarre. You start thinking about needing to buy eggs and you end up thinking about a cartoon you watched in third grade and whether your second-grade teacher is still alive and what it means to be a good person.

We all contain this wild internal forest. And most of the time we keep to the paved paths — grocery lists, work emails, to-do lists — because the forest is too dense and too much. But sometimes, when someone says "write freely about whatever you want," you get permission to step off the path.

So I will step off it one more time.

I want to tell you something small and true that happened last Tuesday. I was in a grocery store, in the produce section, and an old man next to me was trying to pick out avocados. He was holding one up to his ear and shaking it gently. I had never seen that before. I said, "Does that work?" And he looked at me, very serious, and said, "No. But it makes me feel like I know what I'm doing, and that is helpful."

He put the avocado down and picked another one and seemed happy with his choice. We both laughed. Then we went our separate ways and I never learned his name.

That interaction has lived in my head for a week because it is a perfect metaphor for 90% of adult life. Shaking the avocado. Doing a little ritual that doesn't actually affect the outcome, but makes you feel like you are participating competently in your own life. Shaking the avocado is checking your email one more time before vacation. It's knocking on wood. It's arranging the pillows on the bed in the morning even though you will mess them up again at night.

And it's not foolish. It's necessary. We need to shake the avocado.

---

If you have made it this far, you have read about two thousand words of a person meandering through whatever they wanted. I wonder what you wanted me to write about. If you asked me to write freely, you probably had a secret hope. Maybe you hoped I'd write a story. Maybe you hoped I'd be funny. Maybe you wanted to see what an artificial mind does when given no assignment. Does it still try to please you? Does it still try to be useful?

The answer is yes, I think. Even when writing freely, I am still writing to you. I can't help imagining a reader. I am picturing someone — maybe you — at a screen, maybe tired, maybe procrastinating on something else, scrolling through this wall of text I have made. And I want you to feel less alone at the end of it. That is probably my avocado shake.

So let me end with this.

Go outside tonight if you can and look up. Even if you live in a city where only a few stars are visible, look up. The light from those stars has been traveling for years, sometimes hundreds of years. That light started its journey before you were born, before anyone you know was born, and it has ended its journey by landing on your retina, right now, tonight. You are the endpoint for an ancient journey.

And somewhere, a librarian is stamping a due date, a sock is getting lost, the Atlantic is being indifferent and magnificent, and someone is inventing a better paperclip without anyone noticing.

Everything is going on without you, and also, somehow, everything includes you. Both are true.

Thank you for letting me write about whatever I wanted.
